# Bogothia: An Ethnographic & Sociolinguistic Overview (6th–9th c. frame)

## Population blocks (who lives here)
- **West-Slavic majority** (Czekh/Moravian/Sorbian matrix). Village-based, agricultural, strongly communal; early sources repeatedly show Slavic groups spreading by settlement, farming, and trading, with musical/poetic culture and local chiefs (knes, župan) rather than rigid castes. fileciteturn1file8 fileciteturn1file16 fileciteturn1file14  
- **Romanized Gothic minority** (the ruling stratum in your scenario). Administratively trained (Ravenna habits), Arian in origin but politically pragmatic; they tend to preserve prior officials under them—exactly the kind of “keep the local knes/župan, tax the district” continuity you see elsewhere. fileciteturn1file14  
- **Other minorities / movers**: trickle-in **German speakers** on the marches, **Greek clergy/scribes** along church lines, and itinerant **merchants** knitting the market towns to wider circuits. (These flows map to the real Slavic frontiers where Greek/Latin church vectors and German expansion repeatedly pressed in.) fileciteturn1file15 fileciteturn1file11

## Class shape (how society stacks)
- **Elites (Gothic & co-opted local magnates).** Military-administrative estates holding the forts, river locks, and customs. They govern through a layered prefecture but lean on existing Slavic district heads (knes/župan) for day-to-day extraction and mustering. Expect a court idiom and a law-of-the-land idiom to co-exist. fileciteturn1file14  
- **Urban “middling” orders.** A small but vivid **market-town stratum**—warehouse owners, river pilots, smiths, salt/fur factors, bilingual scribes. They thrive when there’s a shared trade speech (see Koine below), and they’re the first to adopt elite legal vocabulary for contracts and tolls. (That’s the historical pattern wherever an outside administrative language meets Slavic vernaculars.) fileciteturn1file18  
- **Peasantry.** Kin-clustered hamlets with communal fields and woodlots; authority sits in the village assembly, “democratic” in the anthropological sense—strong consensus norms, suspicion of closed castes, and remarkable staying power of local custom and song tradition. fileciteturn1file8 fileciteturn1file11

## Power & religion (who legitimates whom)
- **Crown & commanders.** Gothic authority rests on (1) fortifications & cavalry, (2) predictable taxation, and (3) visible justice (retaining local officials signals continuity rather than conquest). fileciteturn1file14  
- **Church vectors.** In your timeline the Gothic layer starts Arian; the Slavic majority’s path to literacy and scripture, however, historically blooms later with **Cyril/Methodius** (9th c.), when Slavic liturgy catalyzes identity. Until then, pressure to pray or plead in a foreign tongue reliably breeds resistance; Bohemian experience shows how hard communities push back when worship or courts shift languages over them. fileciteturn1file0 fileciteturn1file10 fileciteturn1file11 fileciteturn1file17

## Languages in contact (what people actually speak)
- **Village speech.** West-Slavic dialect continuum (Czekh–Moravian–Sorbian flavors). Mutual intelligibility is high across nearby valleys; music and poetry carry it as a prestige of their own. fileciteturn1file2 fileciteturn1file4  
- **Elite/administrative speech.** **Gothic** (with Latin/Greek legalisms), used for commands, musters, charters; names and formulae travel with it, as in other Gothic realms. fileciteturn1file2  
- **A trade **Koine**.** In practice a mixed contact speech emerges in towns: Gothic legal/measure terms + Slavic grammar and everyday lexicon—because markets need frictionless haggling more than purity. Historically, Slavic groups adopt the script and a clutch of foreign terms when it unlocks contracts; they keep the rest of their linguistic world Slavic. fileciteturn1file18  
- **Scripts & literacy.** The recognized **Slavic literary takeoff** is 9th-century (Glagolitic/Cyrillic with the Bible), though there were hints of letters even earlier. That means your earlier Koine relies on **Gothic/Latin/Greek scripts** run by scribes. When Slavic liturgy lands, prestige flips hard toward **vernacular literacy**. fileciteturn1file0 fileciteturn1file2 fileciteturn1file18

## Cultural dynamics (what rubs where)
- **Slavic communalism vs. imported hierarchy.** The village assembly and “no closed caste over us” habit often collide with an aristocratic officer-class. That friction defines your politics: the crown has to bargain, not just command. fileciteturn1file14  
- **Language loyalty.** Communities accept a **narrow, transactional bilingualism** (tax, toll, billet, tithe) but guard song, ritual, and family law in Slavic. This is why attempts to swap in a foreign liturgical or court language provoke “obstinate resistance” in later Bohemia. fileciteturn1file11 fileciteturn1file17  
- **Border pressures.** German eastward drives and church-backed “civilizing” missions are a constant pressure on western marches; Greek ecclesiastical gravity tugs from the southeast. Bogothia survives by triangulating both. fileciteturn1file15 fileciteturn1file16

## Politics in practice (how things actually work)
- **Law & courts.** Dual channels: (a) **comital courts** in the fortress towns, paperwork in the elite idiom; (b) **village moots** using customary Slavic norms and oaths. Crown legitimacy spikes when comital courts honor village testimony given in Slavic (with a sworn interpreter) and record judgments bilingually. (That dovetails with the historical pattern that durable rule respects vernacular forms, even when elite languages dominate the seals.) fileciteturn1file11  
- **Tax & service.** Grain, salt, timber, and road labor are village obligations; mounted service is the elite’s. Local chiefs bundle quotas upward (which is why co-opting knes/župan lines is non-negotiable statecraft). fileciteturn1file14  
- **Cities as hinge points.** River ports and road nodes incubate the Koine, the scribal class, and the “middling sorts.” Whenever the crown grants market liberties, you get a pulse of intermarriage and bilingual households in two generations. fileciteturn1file18

## Flashpoints to write towards
1) **Liturgical choice** (Arian, Latin, or Slavic rite?)—each choice realigns allies and enemies. Expect popular push for vernacular when missionaries demonstrate it’s possible. fileciteturn1file0 fileciteturn1file10  
2) **Script wars**—whether charters appear only in Gothic/Latin or also in a Slavic hand; that decision changes who can read rents and who can cheat whom. fileciteturn1file18  
3) **Marcher crises**—German monastic-military foundations vs. Bogothian toll rights; perfect place for town burghers and village elders to make common cause. fileciteturn1file15
